title: Check a chimney before the first fire
summary: Before the first fire after storms, an earthquake or years of disuse, look the chimney over from the ground, the house, the bottom and the top, sweep it and smoke-test it. A blocked or cracked flue puts smoke and carbon monoxide in the house and lets heat into the walls; an unlined, bracket, Type A or broken chimney needs a liner or a separate insulated chimney instead.

materials.item: Bright flashlight and a small mirror
Binoculars for the chimney top from the ground
Rope and a heavy ball or weight about 25 mm (1 in) narrower than the flue
Board or sheet metal and tape to seal the fireplace opening, and something to cover the chimney top
Battery CO alarm and smoke alarm for the room

steps.text: Walk all the way round from the ground, with binoculars if you have them. Look for a lean, bulges, cracks, loose or missing bricks, crumbling mortar near the top, dark or white stains and brick faces splitting off (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat).
steps.warn: A cracked or leaning chimney can fall: keep people out from under it, don't sleep beside it, and don't lean a ladder on it (FEMA chimneys, MU G1735).

steps.text: Work out what kind of chimney it is (table in the notes). Unlined, bracket-mounted, old Type A and air-cooled chimneys are not for wood: stop here and read 'When it can't be used' (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat).
Inside, follow the chimney through every room, closet and the attic. Smoke or tar stains on it show leaks (AD J); look for corrosion and decay where it is hidden (CMHC wood heat).
Open the cleanout door at the base and look for tile fragments, liquid stains, nests and debris. Clear it and shut it tight afterwards (NRCan wood heating).

Work the fireplace damper and check the flue is open before any fire (CPSC 611). The plate is usually held by a couple of cotter pins and can be brittle from heat (MU G1735), so a seized one may have to be taken out: go gently (our suggestion).

From the roof, only if the ground check passed: look at the crown, the cap, the top courses of brick, and down the flue with a flashlight; from below use a mirror (MU G1735, CSIA white paper, NRCan wood heating).
steps.warn: Snow and ice hide vents and make roof and rungs slippery (Alaska DOL snow): in winter check from below with a mirror and keep off the roof. Ladder tied or footed, someone with you, no wind or dark. See the fall hazard card.

steps.text: Lower a heavy ball about 25 mm (1 in) narrower than the flue on a rope from the top to the bottom. If it stops, clear the blockage and try again (AD J).
steps.warn: Not in a flexible metal liner, which a ball or the wrong brush can damage (AD J).

steps.text: Sweep the flue, and look at what comes down: lots of brick or liner pieces mean it needs repair (AD J). See [Sweeping](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping).

Smoke-test it with flue-testing pellets as in the notes: warm the flue, light the pellets, seal the bottom, cover the top once smoke flows, and check the whole length inside and out for at least 5 minutes, then take both covers off and let the smoke clear (AD J).
steps.warn: Cover the top only over smoke pellets, never over a real fire.

steps.text: Forceful plumes or lots of smoke from a joint, a crack, the attic or another flue mean a fault: don't use it until it's fixed or relined (AD J).

Decide: sound and lined, use it; unlined, cracked or damaged, reline it with a certified stainless liner or run a separate insulated chimney (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat). See [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).

First fire: CO alarm and smoke alarm working and a small fire to start (Drolet Part 1), with someone watching the chimney outside and in the attic for smoke. See [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

notes:
## Why bother
A chimney you haven't used in years, or one that has been through a storm or an earthquake, can be blocked, cracked or loose. A blocked flue, a faulty damper or a chimney that isn't venting puts smoke and carbon monoxide in the house (NRCan wood heating). A cracked or missing liner lets heat reach the wood around it: in 1940s tests, wood touching the outside of an unlined chimney carrying 540 °C (1,000 °F) flue gas caught fire after three and a half hours (CSIA white paper). Flues get blocked by nests, bits of brick, liner and chimney pot, and soot and tar, and the exposed top of a chimney decays fastest (AD J). Lightning, weathering, freeze and thaw, moisture, flue gases and settling all damage chimneys too (CSIA white paper).

## What kind of chimney is it?
| You see | What it is | Fit for a wood stove? |
|---|---|---|
| Brick or stone with clay tiles showing at the top | Lined masonry chimney | Yes, if sound (CMHC wood heat), with no other appliance on that flue (Drolet Part 1) |
| Brick or stone with no liner inside, just brick or mortar | Unlined masonry | No; some can take a certified stainless liner (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat) |
| Brick chimney that starts partway up a wall, sitting on wood or brick brackets, not on its own foundation | Bracket chimney | No, and it can't be upgraded (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat) |
| Double-wall stainless pipe with a label reading ULC S629 or UL 103HT; DuraTech's 150 mm (6 in) flue is about 200 mm (8 in) round outside, other makers differ | Insulated 650 °C factory-built chimney | Yes, with that maker's parts (NRCan wood heating, DuraVent DTC) |
| Metal chimney with no ULC S629 or UL 103HT label, maybe with a painted or square outer casing and walls about 25 mm (1 in) thick, made for oil furnaces and used before the early 1980s | Possibly an old Type A | No: it can't take a chimney fire (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat) |
| Metal chimney of a decorative factory-built fireplace that is cooled by air between its layers | Air-cooled chimney | Never connect a stove to it (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat) |

The sources differ on the Type A date: NRCan says used before 1983, CMHC before 1981, so a metal chimney put in around 1981 to 1983 could be either (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat). CMHC says a painted outside or a square casing could mean Type A, but looks don't settle it. A metal chimney without a ULC S629 or UL 103HT label is not one to burn wood in: Drolet's manual connects its stove only to a Type HT chimney listed to those standards, or to lined masonry (Drolet Part 1). Gas B-vent isn't a chimney for wood: its maker says not to use any gas vent on oil or wood-burning appliances (DuraVent B-vent). Stovepipe only connects a stove to a chimney (NRCan wood heating): see [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).

## Warning signs
- **From outside:** brick or mortar crumbling near the top, dark or white stains on the brick, brick faces splitting off (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat); a cracked crown (failed crowns are among the commonest causes of chimney decay, CSIA white paper); no cap (every chimney should have one to stop wind blowing smoke back down, NRCan wood heating).
- **Inside the house:** smoke or tar stains on the chimney breast or in the attic show leaks (AD J); check the chimney where it is hidden, in the attic, walls and chase, where corrosion and decay happen unseen (CMHC wood heat).
- **At the cleanout:** pieces of tile and liquid stains (NRCan wood heating).
- **Down the flue:** cracks or missing pieces in the liner (CMHC wood heat); on a metal chimney, rust stains on the shell and bulges or corrosion in the liner (NRCan wood heating).
- **Signs of an old chimney fire:** puffy creosote, warped metal, cracked or collapsed tiles, a discoloured cap, cracks in the outside masonry, smoke through mortar joints (CSIA preventing). See [Sweeping and chimney fires](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping).

## Nests and animals
Bird nests and debris can block a flue and stop it working (CSIA homeowner, AD J). From southeast Saskatchewan to Nova Scotia, chimney swifts nest in brick and stone chimneys and are protected by law (ECCC swift, Birds Canada swifts). ECCC puts their nesting at mid-May to mid-August; Birds Canada asks people not to use, clean or repair the chimney from 15 April to 15 October (ECCC swift, Birds Canada swifts). By the heating season they've flown south, and their nest is a cup about 10 cm wide glued to the wall, which Birds Canada says won't block the chimney or start a fire (Birds Canada swifts). Raccoons and squirrels get into chimneys too (Birds Canada swifts), and a narrow metal liner can trap animals inside, so keep it capped (Birds Canada swifts). Treat droppings and dead animals with the care on the [biohazard card](#browse/hazards/biohazard).

## Storms and earthquakes
Masonry chimneys in wood-frame houses are extremely vulnerable to earthquakes; older unreinforced ones with worn mortar are the worst, and some that had already been damaged and rebuilt collapsed in the next quake (FEMA chimneys). Repairing an old unreinforced chimney to modern standards is generally not practical, and patching cracks or repointing does little; the best fix is a metal flue (FEMA chimneys). Until then, spend as little time next to the chimney as you can, inside and out, and don't sleep beside it (FEMA chimneys). After a big storm, look for the same signs as above, plus a moved or missing cap.

## The smoke test
The UK building rules give a proper method (AD J, smoke test I):
1. Sweep the flue first (AD J).
2. Close the doors and windows of the room. Warm the flue with an electric heater or blowlamp so it draws; a big or cold flue can take more than 10 minutes (AD J).
3. Light flue-testing smoke pellets in the fireplace or stove. When smoke starts, seal the fireplace opening with a board taped at the edges, or shut the stove's door and air controls (AD J).
4. When smoke comes freely out of the top, cover the top. Check the whole length inside and out, attic included, for at least 5 minutes (AD J). Then take the covers off the top and the bottom (AD J), open the windows and let the smoke clear before any real fire. Whoever covers the top is on the roof, so the ladder and winter rules above apply.
5. Smoke out of a neighbouring flue means the flues leak into each other. Smoke can come out well away from the fault (AD J).

Wisps at joints aren't necessarily a fault, but forceful plumes or large amounts of smoke mean a broken joint or damaged section (AD J). Only ever cover the top over smoke pellets, never over a real fire: the smoke and carbon monoxide would have nowhere to go but the house.

No pellets? The second test in the same rules lets the smoke rise with the draft and watches that it comes freely out of the top, doesn't spill into the room, and doesn't leak anywhere along the chimney (AD J). A small first fire watched the same way is the closest substitute, but it is our adaptation and a riskier one: the rule's test uses smoke pellets and says an appliance should not be under fire during it (AD J), while a real fire sends hot gas and CO through any leak. Only do it once the chimney has passed the visual checks and the sweep. Start with a few sheets of newspaper, keep the CO alarm working, put one person outside and one in the attic, and put the fire out at once if smoke shows anywhere but the chimney top.

## When it can't be used, and what to do instead
Don't burn in it if it is unlined, a bracket chimney, a Type A or an air-cooled chimney, if the liner is cracked or broken, or if it leans, has loose bricks or failed the smoke test (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat, CSIA white paper). The options:
- **Reline it** with a certified stainless liner, rigid or flexible, from the stove to the top; this is also the fix for a chimney damaged by a fire or too big for the stove (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat).
- **Leave it** and run a separate insulated 650 °C chimney through the wall or roof (NRCan wood heating): see [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).
- **A Type A chimney** should be replaced with 650 °C chimney as soon as possible (CMHC wood heat, NRCan wood heating).
- **Neither possible?** Then the chimney stays unused: burning in a faulty one risks smoke, CO and fire inside the walls (NRCan wood heating, CSIA white paper). Heat one small room another way: see [Get through winter in one heated room](#guides/skill_staying_warm).

## The damper
CPSC says to check that the flue is open before any fire (CPSC 611). The plate is usually held by a couple of cotter pins and can be brittle from heat (MU G1735), so a seized one may have to come out: our suggestion, since MU describes removing it for sweeping. It stays open until the fire is completely out and the ashes are cold (Calgary fireplaces): see [Fireplace heating](#guides/skill_fireplace_heating).
